fields.name: Продукт-1
fields.description: У основателя австрийской экономической школы Карла Менгера учению о товаре посвящена 7 глава его «Оснований политической экономии». Менгер различает товар и экономическое благо. Определяя товар, как экономическое благо, предназначенное для продажи, и теряющее свойства товара при попадании к конечному потребителю, он впервые разграничивает эти два экономические понятия. Также он описывает различия понятия товар в обыденном и научном смысле. В обыденной речи товарами называют предметы, которые производитель или торговец готов обменять, причём это понятие ограничивается только вещами, с исключением из них денег. В научном изложении товаром называют любые блага, предназначенные для обмена, независимо от их материальности, способности к передвижению, их характера как продуктов труда, независимо от лиц, предлагающих их для продажи. Также приводится описание основных свойств товаров, как экономической категории — границы способности товаров к сбыту, степени способности к сбыту и способность товара к обращению. Под границами способности товара к сбыту понимается суммарный потребительский спрос. Так, согласно Менгеру, спрос на сочинение о языке индейцев Латинской Америки тупи не превысит 600 экземпляров при минимальной цене, в то время как граница способности к сбыту произведений Шекспира превышает сотни тысяч. Степень способности товара к сбыту важна для товаров, которые не имеют самостоятельного значения, а нужны лишь как составные части других. Менгер приводит пример пружин для механических часов и манометров. Какова бы ни была их цена, количество продаваемых пружин будет зависеть только от производства часов и манометров. В то же время золото и серебро практически не имеют пределов способности к сбыту

fields.description_en:
The founder of the Austrian economic school, Carl Menger, devotes Chapter 7 of his “Foundations of Political Economy” to the doctrine of the commodity. Menger distinguishes between a commodity and an economic good. Defining a product as an economic good intended for sale and losing the properties of the product when it reaches the final consumer, he for the first time distinguishes between these two economic concepts. He also describes the differences between the concept of goods in the ordinary and scientific sense. In everyday speech, goods are items that a manufacturer or trader is willing to exchange, and this concept is limited only to things, with the exception of money. In a scientific presentation, a commodity is any good intended for exchange, regardless of their materiality, ability to move, their nature as products of labor, regardless of the persons offering them for sale. A description of the basic properties of goods as an economic category is also provided - the boundaries of the ability of goods to be sold, the degree of ability to be sold and the ability of the product to circulate. The limits of a product's ability to sell are understood as total consumer demand. Thus, according to Menger, the demand for an essay on the language of the Tupi Indians of Latin America will not exceed 600 copies at a minimum price, while the limit of the ability to sell Shakespeare's works exceeds hundreds of thousands. The degree of ability of a product to be sold is important for goods that do not have independent significance, but are needed only as components of others. Menger gives the example of springs for mechanical watches and pressure gauges. Whatever their price, the number of springs sold will depend only on the production of watches and pressure gauges. At the same time, gold and silver have virtually no limits to their ability to be sold.

Quo nulla voluptas et voluptate nesciunt et laudantium nihil et accusantium tempore qui deserunt distinctio. Nam consectetur adipisci ut voluptas ducimus aut alias velit qui nemo numquam! Rem placeat possimus vel laboriosam porro eos neque odit a nihil voluptates ut totam dicta est voluptatum consequatur! Eum molestiae sint sit nostrum maxime qui consectetur laborum eum alias debitis ut delectus numquam.

fields.description_en: The founder of the Austrian economic school, Carl Menger, devotes Chapter 7 of his “Foundations of Political Economy” to the doctrine of the commodity. In everyday speech, goods are items that a manufacturer or trader is willing to exchange, and this concept is limited only to things, with the exception of money. In a scientific presentation, a commodity is any good intended for exchange, regardless of their materiality, ability to move, their nature as products of labor, regardless of the persons offering them for sale. A description of the basic properties of goods as an economic category is also provided - the boundaries of the ability of goods to be sold, the degree of ability to be sold and the ability of the product to circulate. At the same time, gold and silver have virtually no limits to their ability to be sold.

fields.description_en: The founder of the Austrian economic school, Carl Menger, devotes Chapter 7 of his “Foundations of Political Economy” to the doctrine of the commodity. Menger distinguishes between a commodity and an economic good. Defining a product as an economic good intended for sale and losing the properties of the product when it reaches the final consumer, he for the first time distinguishes between these two economic concepts. He also describes the differences between the concept of goods in the ordinary and scientific sense. In everyday speech, goods are items that a manufacturer or trader is willing to exchange, and this concept is limited only to things, with the exception of money. In a scientific presentation, a commodity is any good intended for exchange, regardless of their materiality, ability to move, their nature as products of labor, regardless of the persons offering them for sale. A description of the basic properties of goods as an economic category is also provided - the boundaries of the ability of goods to be sold, the degree of ability to be sold and the ability of the product to circulate. The limits of a product's ability to sell are understood as total consumer demand. Thus, according to Menger, the demand for an essay on the language of the Tupi Indians of Latin America will not exceed 600 copies at a minimum price, while the limit of the ability to sell Shakespeare's works exceeds hundreds of thousands. The degree of ability of a product to be sold is important for goods that do not have independent significance, but are needed only as components of others. Menger gives the example of springs for mechanical watches and pressure gauges. Whatever their price, the number of springs sold will depend only on the production of watches and pressure gauges. At the same time, gold and silver have virtually no limits to their ability to be sold.

fields.review_en: A bag is a paper or plastic bag rolled into a cone. Initially, this was the name for small bags (kulebyaki), which sellers made by hand from paper for bulk products (nuts, seeds). In modern colloquial language, this word is often used as a synonym for an ordinary plastic bag or pouch.

fields.review: Бутылка — это узкогорлый высокий сосуд, преимущественно цилиндрической формы, предназначенный для долговременного или кратковременного хранения жидкостей и сыпучих веществ. В русском языке слово заимствовано через польский язык (butelka) из латыни (butticula — бочонок). До введения метрической системы в России «бутылка» также служила официальной мерой объема жидкостей: винная составляла 1/16 ведра (около 0,77 л), а водочная или пивная — 1/20 ведра (около 0,6 л).

fields.review_en: A bottle is a narrow-necked, tall vessel, mostly cylindrical in shape, designed for long-term or short-term storage of liquids and bulk substances. In Russian, the word is borrowed through the Polish language (butelka) from Latin (butticula - barrel). Before the introduction of the metric system in Russia, a “bottle” also served as an official measure of the volume of liquids: wine was 1/16 of a bucket (about 0.77 l), and vodka or beer was 1/20 of a bucket (about 0.6 l).
